kf1.tip: Choose a business you know, invent a selling price, variable cost per unit and fixed costs, then work out its contribution per unit and break-even in units.
kf1.note: A good answer shows two steps you can check. First, take your selling price minus your variable cost per unit to get contribution per unit. Second, divide your fixed costs by that contribution to get break-even in units. Oakleaf shows the pattern: £3.50 minus £1.10 gives £2.40, and £1,200 divided by £2.40 gives 500 lattes. If your selling price is below your variable cost, there is no contribution, so change your figures.

kf2.tip: Argue for and against the claim that the project with the higher ARR is always the better choice, using timing of returns and risk, then decide.
kf2.note: A strong answer says a higher ARR does mean a bigger average yearly return, which is why Oakleaf would pick 45% over 30% if the risk was similar. Against this, ARR ignores when returns arrive, so year 5 profits count the same as year 1. It also ignores risk: 30% on a reckless venture is worse than 15% on a safe one. Most conclude it is not always better. The trap is comparing the percentages and stopping there.

cs1.tip: Cover the figures, then predict whether Oakleaf's break-even rises or falls when rent goes up £300, the latte goes to £4.00 and variable cost goes to £1.40.
cs1.note: When rent goes up, break-even rises to 625 lattes, because fixed costs, the top of the formula, are bigger. When the latte goes to £4.00, break-even falls to 414, because each latte now contributes £2.90 instead of £2.40. When variable cost goes to £1.40, break-even rises to 572, because contribution falls to £2.10. If you got that last one wrong, remember that a cost rise shrinks contribution, so the business needs more sales.
